book: 283 - Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am

chapters.file: ch25 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Heaps uses the loaded question a stranger asks a tattooed person ('aren't you afraid of being stuck with it?') to raise the freedom-versus-determinism problem, then rejects Kant's Critique of Practical Reason solution of an 'alternate nature' of rational autonomy because it quarantines free choice from the physical act of being inked. He argues instead for an 'embodied freedom' that rests on but is not determined by biology, illustrated by deciding, saving for, sitting through, and healing a tattoo. He closes with Socrates' 'know thyself' and 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' making self-examination the way to develop the effective willingness that real freedom requires.

chapters.file: ch26 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
ch27 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Lee argues that tattooing is a performative 'practice of writing' whose meaning always exceeds its origin, comparing Holocaust survivor Tova Friedman's Auschwitz number 'A27633' with the Suicide Girl Jaylin's chosen feminist ink. Drawing on Judith Butler's account of the body as a site of inscription and counter-inscription, and Walter Benjamin's 'Critique of Violence' distinguishing law-making from law-preserving force, she claims Friedman's tattoo resists the Nazi law itself while Jaylin's only satirizes heteropatriarchy. She then invokes Baudrillard's 'ecstasy of communication' and the obscene to show tattooing can desubjectify by dissolving the embodied self into pornographic information.

chapters.file: ch28 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Decker reads Ray Bradbury's 'The Illustrated Man' (William Phelps, whose witch-inked tattoo of murdering his wife Lisabeth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy) and 'The Illustrated Woman' (Emma and Willy Fleet's shared delusion of an invisible masterpiece) to ask whether 'the body is our fate.' He aligns Phelps's predetermined tattoo with Alvin Goldman's 'Book of Life' thought experiment about foreknowledge and lost free will, and with Foucault's claim that power socially constructs docile bodies. Against this fatalism he sets George Herbert Mead's creative social self, 'taking the attitude of the other,' arguing tattooing is a plural renegotiation of identity rather than a fixed inscription.

chapters.file: ch29 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
ch30 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Baker dismisses common objections to tattoos (shallow individuality, permanence, ugliness) as aesthetic rather than moral, then uses Greco-Roman virtue ethics—quoting Seneca's Moral Epistles on the soul, the balanced psyche, and matching one's norms to one's motivations—to isolate her real target: the 'tough tattoo.' She argues that a badass or tough-guy tattoo appropriates an outlaw subculture's imagery and, per Seneca's warning that approving a little violence approves it all, cultivates a vicious rather than virtuous psyche. Recalling friends who bragged about beatings, she invokes Socratic self-examination ('know thyself') to test whether looking tough is an accurate or worthy self-representation.

chapters.file: ch31 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Miori, a palliative-care physician assistant and clinical bioethicist, separates personal ethics, professional ethics, and bioethics, then evaluates tattooing through Beauchamp and Childress's principles—especially autonomy (intention, understanding, freedom from outside influence) weighed against risk versus benefit. He concludes tattooing is bioethically fine because safer pigments and market forces reduced its disease risks and because autonomy makes 'to ink or not' the patient's own call, echoing a Millian liberty that one's choice not harming others is 'none of your beeswax.' He ends by defending the memorial tattoo as therapeutic 'memory remodeling' that gluing a positive event in place with pain can make good for you.

chapters.file: ch32 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Woods asks whether the claim 'tattooing is immoral' can be defended, taking Adolf Loos's 1908 'Ornament and Crime' (tattooed free men are latent criminals or degenerate aristocrats) as his provocation. He rejects Loos's equation of tattooing with murder, since tattooing is voluntary and self-regarding, but resists the liberal 'sovereign self' reply drawn from Mill's On Liberty by arguing autonomy and the body are relational, not absolute, so a person's self-regarding choices remain open to reasoned challenge and even regulation. He proposes regret evidence in informed consent and an age-25 minimum, concluding tattooing is a matter of both taste and morality.

chapters.file: ch33 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
ch34 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Barkman, prompted by his wedding guests' shared discomfort with his best man's tattooed arms, sets out to dispel a 'Christian Confucian confusion' that reads piety as requiring a tattoo-free body. He shows Leviticus 19:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 condemn tattooing only where it signals allegiance to impure cults or misuse of the body, not tattooing in itself, and that Confucius's Hsiao King injunction against wounding the body one receives from one's parents was linked to tattoos only by Han Chinese racism against tattooed minorities. Citing General Yue Fei's mother inking loyalty on his back, he concludes ink can even be pious, though a child under a parent's legitimate authority owes obedience if forbidden it.

chapters.file: ch35 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Lynch, a tattooed Buddhist philosophy professor, tests his largely Buddhist body art (an Om-mani-padme-hum armband, Bodhidharma, the Buddha's face, the eight-spoked Wheel and lotus, a double-vajra) against the Buddha's Three Marks of Existence. He argues a 'permanent' tattoo need not contradict impermanence any more than Gruzalski's washed-away sandcastle if approached mindfully, that custom ink need not reify a self given the chariot analogy of no-self (which he links to Hume's bundle view), and that the pain of tattooing directly instantiates dukkha and can become an object of meditation and compassion. Mindful tattooing, he concludes, can itself be authentic Buddhist practice.

chapters.file: ch36 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Arp frames a dialogue between two ex-seminarians who once got matching cross tattoos: Bill, who added more Christian ink, and Rick, who now regrets his cross as an atheist secular humanist. Bill defends God via Aquinas's combined proof from motion and causation—tracing the tattoo artist and even the Big Bang back to an unmoved mover / uncaused cause—and the 'three Ms' of mind, meaning, and morality, gesturing toward Paley-style design. Rick counters with a self-sustaining infinite series, the interaction problem between a supernatural God and nature, and the charge that God is a comforting fiction, so morality and meaning are humanly made rather than divinely guaranteed.

chapters.file: ch37 - TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am.md

holes.name: George Herbert Mead
holes.what: American pragmatist social psychologist who held the self is constructed through social interaction by 'taking the attitude of the other.'
holes.why: Chapter 28's constructive counter to Foucault's and Goldman's fatalism rests on Mead's creative social self, quoting Mind, Self and Society at length, and no taxonomy philosopher covers him.
